newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines throws defector hunters off trail.
newsitem.headline: Philippines throws defector hunters off trail.

text.p: A slew of rumours and conflicting tip-offs have enabled the Philippines to cast a smokescreen over the whereabouts of top North Korean defector Hwang Jang-yop and protect him from potential assassins.

Immigrations agents at airports around the country remained on full alert on Friday for possible Pyongyang hitmen as the highest ranked North Korean official to flee the Stalinist state began his fourth day in hiding.
"Don't underestimate the North Koreans. They will wait until things cool down," an Asian diplomat told Reuters. "He may not be safe even in Seoul."

Pyongyang's top ideologue defected to the South Korean consulate in Beijing on February 12 and had languished there for more than a month until a Chinese jetliner spirited him into the former U.S. Clark airbase north of Manila on Tuesday.
A South Korean foreign ministry official said on Thursday that Hwang would remain in the Philippines at least until the start of next month.

Since his secrecy-shrouded flight into Clark, Philippine military officials have sent dozens of Filipino and foreign journalists scrambling all over the country with tip-offs and leaks on where Hwang was supposed to be.
One "leak" had him in the northern mountain city of Baguio where he was supposed to be staying either at the presidential summer mansion or at the Philippine Military Academy (PMA).
Others said he had been flown from Clark to the tightly guarded intelligence compound of the armed forces headquarters offices headquarters in Manila.
Still others said he had been moved from Baguio to the former U.S. Subic naval base, which is now a bustling freeport.
One colonel said his information was that Hwang might be on central Mindoro island.
"We don't know where he is. We don't have any idea," a PMA spokesman told Reuters, adding it was possible the welter of information being fed to the media was only "a smokescreen."
A senior Philippine diplomat said ensuring Hwang's safety was a "top secret operation" and that it was possible the military was deliberately leaking false information to mislead journalists.

The paranoia over Hwang's safety prompted immigration officials on Thursday to mount a tight watch on possible assassins who might arrive at the Manila international airport or other international airports around the country.
The alert included putting up two posters on a bulletin board at Manila airport's immigration office with the pictures of 22 alleged members of the guerrilla Japanese Red Army.
One poster with the photographs of seven alleged Japanese extremists was captioned, "Red Army faction in North Korea."
"We are on red alert," a senior immigration official said.
He said immigration agents around the country had been ordered to give special attention to arriving orientals, specially those carrying Korean, Chinese, Vietnamese and Japanese passports.
Military sources suggested it was useless for the media to try and locate Hwang.
"This is a top-secret operation. Why do you still keep looking for him," one official said.
North Korea has a history of deadly attacks against arch-rival South Korea, with which it is still in Cold War confrontation.
Three days after Hwang sought asylum in Beijing, a North Korean defector was fatally shot near Seoul. He was found by assassins despite having cosmetic surgery to hide his identity.
